description: Working on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator - Interested in helping the public and those working on a mission compare landing sites and dates quickly, while making an interactive interface.
summary: LunaLink is an intuitive, interactive 3D web application designed to bridge the gap between complex technical lunar datasets and rapid, accessible decision-making. It utilizes raw ephemeris and topography data to help students, educators, and professionals in the field understand how changing different metrics affects the optimization of the landing site. It will tell you if a lander will get sunlight for power and visibility to Earth for communication, and will tell you if it is a good spot, risky, or if the lander is lost. You can see why a site fails, compare sites, plan your own mission, and stand on the surface as the mission plays hour by hour. It features site comparisons, real-time horizon and sky-view projections, and automated feasibility metrics for solar power generation and direct-to-Earth communication windows. Mission planning schedules frequently shift due to hardware challenges or launch delays, requiring agile trade-off analyses. LunaLink accelerates this process for mission planners while serving as an engaging educational tool to empower students and the public to explore the constraints of lunar exploration.
details:
• LunaLink allows users to explore landing sites, understand factors that affect their optimization, and create custom missions to understand and analyze the specialized data visually. It allows you to analyse data from landing sites, suggests a better date to try, and provides a terrain cross-section of what block the Sun or Earth, with an antenna mast from 1-10m. It ranks every site by % of the mission with the Sun, Earth, and with both. It also contains a compass showing where the Sun and Earth are, and which way the shadows fall.
  • How it Works: The horizon is measured as the highest ground angle from all directions. The margin for Sun and Earth clearance is measured by subtracting the horizon height, with a positive value meaning it clears the ridge. The Earth is considered visible when its centre clears the horizon. The verdict of how successful the mission will eb is calculated through the battery, and percentage of Earth and Sun visibility. If the Sun and Earth are both over 85%, it is considered a good spot, anything else is considered risky. If the battery hits 0%, the lander is lost. The battery charges +3% per hour in full sun and drains 2% per hour in the dark. 
  • The languages used to develop this project consisted of plain HTML, CSS, and javascript. The 3D was created with Three.js with custom GLSL shaders for the terrain, Sun, Earth, and stars. The audio tools included web audio API for radio tone. Data processing was done with Python 3 + NumPy for terrain.py, horizons.py, export_scene.py, etc. Hosting / Cl was with Vercel, and auto-deployed by Github Actions on every merge. The translation tool was implemented through google translate widget to 34 languages. 
  • Our team considered three main factors that affect landing site analysis. The Sun provides illumination and power for solar panels, meaning we had to showcase the total sunlight duration, time to the next sunset and sunrise, the longest continuous darkness period, and the solar elevation angle. The position of Earth is important for visibility and to maximize direct-to-Earth communication without requiring relay satellites. This is measured through the Earth visibility duration, longest communication blackout, elevation angle, and Earthset. Finally, as this is all relative to the Moon, local terrain and obstructions are important, as they could block the Sun or Earth even if they are in optimal positions relative to the horizontal plane at the landing site.
  • Through the ‘Explore’ mode, users are able to look through provided landing sites and understand changes caused by launch delays as well as when and why the Sun or Earth is blocked. It also shows the elevation angles of both celestial bodies, local terrain slope, and if the clearance changes with variable antenna heights in the ‘Why’ section. This tab also enables users to see landing site condition changes throughout the week at a glance. The positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the Moon are always available, and there is a provided time-lapse of the positions changing throughout the calendar year, and its effects on the Moon. 
  • Our team’s approach to this challenge was to not only show data, but help people understand how changing factors affects the landing site. The ‘Plan’ mode empowers users to choose custom landing coordinates, mission duration, date range, and battery of the rover. These custom missions can be saved and compared, helping users understand how to optimize for a mission site and date, and explore beyond the provided presets. 
  • The site comparison feature shows the percentage of time the Sun is illuminating the base, the percentage of time the Earth is visible, as well as when both of these events overlap. This was meant to make clear connections between the data, helping users understand how to optimize for a landing site, rather than having to analyze individual landing sites. 
  • LunaLink eliminates the complexity and steep learning curve of navigating multiple specialist tools, allowing mission planners to quickly evaluate alternative sites or dates when launch delays or hardware challenges force schedule shifts. It also empowers students, educators, and the general public to understand why public-funded space missions are deeply sensitive to small changes and what factors contribute to mission planning. By creating a website application to make analysis of this data more accessible, we aim to increase understanding and interest in STEM and space exploration, which would in turn help fund space programs.
